Implementing a Parental Anxiety Reduction Protocol (PARP) in the Perioperative Period.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Parents and children often experience anxiety when a child undergoes a surgical procedure. Parental anxiety may influence the child's perioperative experience and has been associated with increased child anxiety, which is linked to adverse postoperative outcomes, including an increased incidence of postoperative delirium, higher pain scores, and a greater need for intraoperative analgesia. The effects of untreated preoperative anxiety may extend beyond the immediate perioperative period and contribute to maladaptive behaviors at home. The purpose of this project was to implement and evaluate a structured protocol designed to reduce parental anxiety during the pediatric perioperative period. DESIGN: An evidence-based quality improvement project guided by the Knowledge-to-Action model was conducted over a 3-month period at a Level I pediatric trauma hospital. The project targeted parents of children aged 2 to 10 years undergoing outpatient surgical procedures. METHODS: A Parental Anxiety Reduction Protocol was developed using three evidence-based interventions implemented across the perioperative continuum. The protocol included an educational pamphlet provided to parents at registration, play therapy for children in the preoperative setting, and a meditation video provided to parents during the intraoperative phase. Parental anxiety was measured before and after implementation of the protocol using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory-6 (STAI-6). Pre- and postintervention anxiety scores were statistically analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of the protocol. FINDINGS: Implementation of the Parental Anxiety Reduction Protocol resulted in a statistically significant reduction in parental anxiety scores. Postintervention STAI-6 scores were significantly lower than preintervention scores (P < .001), demonstrating that the multimodal perioperative intervention was effective in reducing parental anxiety. CONCLUSIONS: A structured, evidence-based perioperative protocol incorporating parental education, pediatric play therapy, and parental meditation significantly reduced parental anxiety among parents of children undergoing outpatient surgery. Reducing parental anxiety may also help mitigate pediatric perioperative anxiety and contribute to improved perioperative experiences and outcomes for children and their families.

papers.title: From illness to stillness: on becoming (a) patient.
papers.abstract: Illness is often understood as a disruption of ordinary temporality, fracturing narrative continuity, constricting horizons of possibility, and immersing sufferers in the slow, uncertain rhythms of waiting. Drawing on phenomenology, existential philosophy, pathography, and East Asian wisdom traditions, this article examines the relationship between growing ill and growing still, being a patient and developing patience. While contemporary accounts of illness have richly described experiences of temporal distortion, boredom, loss, and desynchronization, less attention has been given to the possibility that illness may also cultivate forms of composure, attentiveness, and moral endurance. We argue that the temporal disruptions associated with illness, disability, and aging, by interrupting the accelerated rhythms of late modern life, can create opportunities for stillness, presence, and renewed responsiveness. For this we coin the term st/illness. We also distinguish between being a patient, insofar as it connotes passivity and dependence, and being patient, an active virtue that allows one to meet the temporal demands imposed by bodily limitation and breakdown. While not minimizing or romanticizing the physical and emotional suffering often associated with illness, the article explores how illness can also function as a pharmakon in the Greek sense-both poison and remedy-revealing possibilities for resonance, contemplative presence, and existential transformation. This offers a framework for understanding how patients may sometimes flourish within, rather than despite the altered temporalities of illness.
